---
title: "Financial Markets and Behaviors"

## Introduction and Overview {#sec-intro}

This chapter explores the structure of financial markets and their empirical properties.
Two major questions run through it:

- Are markets **efficient** — that is, do they correctly reflect all available information?
- Do financial prices behave like simple **random walks**, or do they present recognizable structures?

To answer these, we examine trading venues, available instruments, traded volumes, and finally the
**stylised facts** (*stylised facts*) — that is, the empirical regularities universally observed on financial markets.

---

## Market Evolution {#sec-evolution}

### Increasing Volatility over the Long Term

The observation of the S&P 500 from 1950 to 2012 illustrates a profound transformation of financial markets.
Until the 1970s, markets exhibited relatively **calm and regular** movements.

From the 1980s onwards, several phenomena amplified volatility:

- The progressive **deregulation** of financial markets
- The development of **electronic trading** (*electronic trading*)
- The **globalization** of capital flows
- The appearance of new complex financial instruments (*derivatives*)

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
Moving averages over 1, 2 and 3 years smooth short-term fluctuations and make it possible to
visualize underlying trends. We observe that S&P 500 growth accelerated from
the 1980s onwards, accompanied by much more marked volatility.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway"}
The volatility of financial markets is not stationary: it tends to increase with the
complexification of financial systems and the rise of algorithmic trading.
:::

---

## Efficient Market Hypothesis (Efficient Market Hypothesis — EMH) {#sec-emh}

### Definition and Origin

The **Efficient Market Hypothesis** (*Efficient Market Hypothesis*, EMH) is a fundamental theory of modern finance,
proposed by **Eugene Fama** in 1960 and rewarded with the **Nobel Prize in Economics in 2013**.

It rests on the central idea that financial asset prices **reflect at all times all available information**.
Consequently:

- Investor behaviors are **rational on average**
- It is **impossible to beat the market** systematically
- The price is **always at its fair value** (*fair value*)
- It is **impossible to buy undervalued or overvalued assets** in a durable way

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
If prices instantly incorporate all information, then any abnormal profit opportunity is instantly
eliminated by arbitrageurs. The market functions like an information processing machine.
:::

### The Three Forms of EMH

EMH is articulated in **three forms** according to the extent of information integrated in prices:

#### Weak Form (Weak Form)

The weak form states that prices reflect **all information contained in past prices**.

Implications:

- **Technical analysis** (*technical analysis*) is ineffective — studying historical charts does not generate abnormal returns
- The future of prices is determined solely by **external information** (*exogenous information*)
- The price follows a **random process** (*random walk*) — without new information, there is no predictable trend
- The market **is not necessarily in equilibrium** at every instant

::: {.callout-warning title="Practical Consequence"}
If the weak form is true, trading strategies based on moving averages, Bollinger bands,
support and resistance levels have no systematic added value. Any mechanical rule derived from past
prices is doomed to long-term inefficiency.
:::

#### Semi-Strong Form (Semi-Strong Form)

The semi-strong form states that prices reflect **all publicly available information**, and this
**instantly** as soon as it is published.

This includes:

- Company earnings announcements
- Central bank decisions
- Published macroeconomic data
- Press releases and analyst analyses

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
If the semi-strong form is valid, it is useless to read financial newspapers for investment
decisions: by the time you read a piece of information, it is already integrated into the price.
:::

#### Strong Form (Strong Form)

The strong form is the most demanding: it states that prices reflect **all information**, whether
**public or private** (*insider information*).

::: {.callout-important title="Radical Implication"}
If the strong form is true, even **insiders** (*insiders*) — persons with confidential
information about a company — cannot realize abnormal profits. This is the least empirically accepted form,
and it directly contradicts the very existence of laws against insider trading.
:::

### Criticisms of EMH

EMH is **widely criticized**, including in its weakest form. Markets present numerous
signs of irrationality:

#### Persistent Overvaluation

Equity markets (*equity*) can remain overvalued relative to **economic fundamentals** (*fundamentals*)
for long periods. The internet bubble (1997–2000) is the most striking illustration.

#### The Case of Great Investors

The durable outperformance of managers like **George Soros** or **Warren Buffett** is difficult to explain
by statistical chance alone. If markets were perfectly efficient, these exceptional performances
over several decades would have a negligible probability.

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
If you flip a coin 1 000 times and always get heads, do you think it's luck? The
durable outperformance of certain investors suggests that there are exploitable inefficiencies.
:::

#### Herding Behaviour (Herding Behaviour)

**Herding behaviour** (*herding behaviour*) describes the tendency of investors to imitate the decisions
of others rather than analyze fundamentals. This phenomenon amplifies market movements and creates
collective inefficiencies.

#### Algorithmic Trading (Algorithmic Trading)

The rise of **algorithmic trading** (*algorithmic trading*, *algo trading*) has profoundly modified the microstructure
of markets. Automatic algorithms react to signals in milliseconds, sometimes amplifying
irrational movements rather than correcting them.

#### Speculative Bubbles (Speculative Bubbles)

**Speculative bubbles** (*speculative bubbles*) constitute perhaps the strongest criticism of EMH:
assets remain systematically mispriced for months or years before a brutal return
to reality.

### Example — The Bitcoin Bubble (Bitcoin Bubble)

The 2013 Bitcoin bubble is a paradigmatic example of irrational market behavior.

Between January 2013 and December 2013:

- The Bitcoin price went from a few dollars to **over 1 000 USD**
- Daily transactions exploded, indicating strong speculation
- The rise was accompanied by massive media interest — a classic signal of market euphoria
- The correction was then brutal and prolonged

::: {.callout-warning title="Lesson from the Bitcoin Bubble"}
The correlation between price and transaction volume indicates that the rise was fueled by
speculation and the FOMO phenomenon (*Fear Of Missing Out*) rather than by fundamental valuation.
This type of dynamic is incompatible with EMH.
:::

### Example — The Flash Crash of May 6, 2010

The **Flash Crash** (*Flash Crash*) of May 6, 2010 is one of the most studied events in modern market history.

In a few minutes, the Dow Jones fell by nearly **998 points (−9.2 %)** before recovering almost all
of its losses in the same session.

Characteristics of the event:

- The fall occurred between **2:30 PM and 3:00 PM** New York time
- Prices of certain stocks temporarily reached absurd levels (a few cents or several thousand dollars)
- Several US exchanges (NASDAQ, NYSE, ARCA, BATS...) recorded similar movements simultaneously
- High-frequency trading algorithms (*High Frequency Trading*, HFT) played a central role in the amplification

::: {.callout-important title="Implications for EMH"}
A collapse of 9 % without new fundamental information, followed by an immediate recovery, is
**incompatible with an efficient market**. It reveals the fragilities introduced by automation and
high-frequency trading in the microstructure of markets.
:::

### A Final Word — The 2013 Nobel Paradox

In 2013, the Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded jointly to **Eugene Fama** (defender of EMH),
**Lars Peter Hansen** and **Robert Shiller** (critic of EMH and theorist of speculative bubbles).

As journalist Christophe Boucher noted in *Le Monde*:

> Economics remains the only discipline where two people can share the same Nobel Prize by telling completely opposite things.

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway"}
There is **no consensus** on the efficiency of financial markets. EMH remains a useful but imperfect
reference framework. The empirical reality of markets contains elements both compatible and incompatible
with this hypothesis.
:::

## Where Do We Exchange? {#sec-lieux}

### Regulated Markets (Regulated Markets / Exchanges)

**Regulated markets** (*exchanges*) are official trading venues, subject to strict
regulation.

Examples:

- **NYSE** — New York Stock Exchange (US equities)
- **LSE** — London Stock Exchange (UK equities)
- **CME** — Chicago Mercantile Exchange (commodity futures)
- **SIX** — SIX Swiss Exchange (Swiss equities)

Characteristics:

- It is a **centralized physical or electronic venue**
- Regulation is **strict**: quotation rules, surveillance, transparency
- There is a **clearing process** (*clearing process*) by a clearing house (*clearing house*)
- **Electronic trading** (*electronic trading*) is growing strongly, but floor trading (*floor trading*) partially persists

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — Clearing"}
The clearing house acts as central counterparty (*Central Counterparty*, CCP) for each transaction.
It guarantees that even if a counterparty defaults, the other will receive its payment. This mechanism considerably reduces
**counterparty risk** (*counterparty risk*).
:::

Brokers (*brokers*) like **Interactive Brokers** allow access to several trading venues
simultaneously from a single interface.

### Over The Counter Markets (Over The Counter — OTC)

**OTC** markets (*Over The Counter*) are decentralized markets where transactions are carried out
directly between parties, without going through a central exchange.

Examples:

- **Oanda** (forex broker)
- Bond markets
- Complex derivatives markets

Characteristics:

- **Less formal** operation and more flexible regulation
- Presence of **market makers** (*market makers*) who propose bid and ask prices (*bid/ask quotes*)
- **Lack of transparency** : prices are not necessarily publicly disseminated
- **Not necessarily a physical venue** — everything happens by phone or electronically

::: {.callout-warning title="OTC Risk"}
OTC markets are riskier because they do not benefit from the protection offered by a clearing
house. In case of counterparty default, fund recovery can be difficult.
:::

### Market Maker vs Broker

It is important to distinguish two types of financial intermediaries:

| Role | Market Maker (*Market Maker*) | Broker (*Broker*) |
|------|----------------------------------|---------------------|
| Example | Oanda | Dukascopy |
| Risk taking | ✅ Yes — holds inventory | ❌ No — no inventory |
| Remuneration | Bid/ask spread | Commission |
| Function | Ensures liquidity | Executes orders |

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Market Maker"}
A market maker earns its living from the **spread**: it buys at a price slightly below the market price
and resells slightly above. In return, it takes the risk of holding positions in inventory.
The more liquid the market, the tighter the spread.
:::

## Financial Assets {#sec-actifs}

### Equities (Equity)

**Equities** (*equity*, *stocks*, *shares*) represent a participation in the capital of a company.

Main characteristics:

- The holder becomes a **shareholder** (*shareholder*) and co-owner of the company
- **Dividends** (*dividends*) are paid periodically (if the company decides so)
- The shareholder bears the **residual risk**: in case of bankruptcy, shareholders are reimbursed last

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
Holding a share is betting on the future growth of a company. The return comes both from
capital gain (*capital gain*) on the share price and from distributed dividends.
:::

### Bonds (Bonds)

**Bonds** (*bonds*) are **debt** securities: the investor lends money to an issuer
who commits to repay it with interest.

Characteristics:

- Can be issued by **States** (*sovereign bonds*, *treasuries*) or **companies** (*corporate bonds*)
- The price of a bond is a **function of its maturity** (*maturity*) and the **coupon payment schedule** (*coupon schedule*)
- Less risky than equities in general (creditors are reimbursed before shareholders)

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — Price / Rate Relationship"}
The price of a bond moves in **inverse** direction to the interest rate: if rates rise, existing
bonds (at lower fixed rates) lose value. This relationship is fundamental in bond management.
:::

### Commodities (Commodities)

**Commodities** (*commodities*) include physical products such as:

- **Agricultural** : wheat (*wheat*), corn (*corn*), coffee, sugar, etc.
- **Energy** : oil (*oil*), natural gas (*natural gas*)
- **Metals** : gold (*gold*), silver (*silver*), copper (*copper*)

Financial particularity:

- Commodities are generally **not traded directly** on financial markets
- **Futures contracts** (*futures*) are used to gain exposure to these assets without having to take physical delivery
- The role of storage and transportation costs is central in valuation

::: {.callout-warning title="Physical Delivery — Warning"}
An investor who buys an oil futures and forgets to close or roll over (*roll over*) their position
before expiration may find themselves obliged to **take delivery of barrels of oil**! This is why
expiration date management is crucial on commodity markets.
:::

### Currencies (Currencies / Foreign Exchange — FX)

**Currencies** (*currencies*) constitute a market in its own right, the **foreign exchange market** (*Forex*, *FX market*).

Fundamental characteristics:

- Currencies are **always quoted in pairs** : EUR/USD, USD/CHF, GBP/USD, etc.
- There is an **interest rate differential** (*interest rate differential*) between the two currencies of a pair
- This differential generates a **carry return** (*carry*) or a **carry cost** depending on the position taken

::: {.callout-important title="Currencies — Backbone of Markets"}
Currencies are the **backbone** (*backbone*) of financial markets. Any international investment
implies a currency conversion, exposing the investor to foreign exchange risk (FX risk).
:::

---

## Transaction Volumes (Considerations About Volumes) {#sec-volumes}

### World Exchanges — Ranking by Volume

The largest world exchanges by equity trading volume in 2013 (in billions of dollars):

| Rank | Exchange | Volume (Bn USD) |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| 1 | NYSE Euronext US | 6 920 |
| 2 | NASDAQ OMX US | 4 748 |
| 3 | Tokyo Stock Exchange | 3 429 |
| 4 | Shanghai Stock Exchange | 1 720 |
| 5 | Shenzhen Stock Exchange | 1 684 |
| 6 | London Stock Exchange | 1 142 |
| 7 | NYSE Euronext Europe | 833 |
| 8 | TMX Group (Canada) | 745 |
| 9 | Hong Kong Exchanges | 677 |
| 10 | Korea Exchange | 676 |

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway"}
US markets (NYSE + NASDAQ) alone represent nearly **60 %** of world equity trading volume,
confirming US dominance in global finance.
:::

### Daily Volume on NASDAQ

To give a concrete order of magnitude, NASDAQ daily statistics in March 2014 indicate:

- Total share volume: between **2 and 2.5 billion shares** per day
- Dollar volume: between **70 and 85 billion dollars** per day
- Total number of transactions: between **9.8 and 11.6 million** per day

These figures illustrate the colossal scale of modern financial markets and the need for robust technological infrastructure to manage them.

### The Foreign Exchange Market — The Largest Market in the World

The foreign exchange market is by far the **most liquid market on the planet**.
According to data from the **BIS** (*Bank for International Settlements*, *Bank for International Settlements*, BIS):

- Daily volume: **approximately 5 000 billion (5 × 10¹²) dollars**
- The **EUR/USD** pair alone represents **25 %** of total volume
- Approximately **50 % of transactions** are **FX swaps** (*FX swaps*)

**Estimation of flow per second on EUR/USD**:

$$\frac{5 \times 10^{12} \times 0.25 \times 0.5}{86\,400 \times 2} \approx 3.6 \text{ million USD/second}$$

The other major pairs (*majors*):

- **USD/JPY** : 18 % of volume
- **GBP/USD** : 9 % of volume

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Size of the FX Market"}
5 000 billion dollars per day means that the foreign exchange market exchanges in **a single day** a
sum exceeding the annual GDP of many countries. No government can durably control this market.
:::

## Main Instruments {#sec-instruments}

### Overview

Financial markets offer a varied range of instruments allowing exposure to different assets
in different forms. The choice of instrument depends on the investment horizon, the desired risk level,
and any hedging need (*hedging*).

### Spot Instrument (Spot)

The **spot** instrument (*spot*) designates the asset itself, transacted and delivered immediately.

Examples:

- A **share** bought on the stock exchange
- An amount of **dollars** bought against euros
- Note: a tonne of physical wheat is generally **not** quoted spot on financial markets

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
Buying spot means buying the real asset, here and now. Delivery can however take a few
business days (typically T+2 for equities).
:::

### Over-The-Counter Forward Contract (Forward)

A **forward contract** (*forward contract*) is an agreement between two parties to **buy or sell an asset
at a price fixed today, at a determined future date**.

Characteristics:

- **Bilateral** contract, negotiated over the counter (*OTC*)
- Flexibility on amount, date and conditions
- Implies a **counterparty risk** (no clearing house)

### Standardized Futures Contract (Futures)

A **futures contract** (*futures contract*) is the **standardized version** of a forward, traded on an
organized exchange with a clearing mechanism.

Differences from the forward:

- **Standardized** contracts: amount, expiration date, underlying asset predefined
- Traded on a **regulated exchange** (*exchange*)
- **Clearing house** (*clearing house*) eliminates counterparty risk
- **Margin calls** (*margin calls*) daily according to price evolution

::: {.callout-warning title="The Roll Over — Watch the Expiration"}
Futures have an **expiration date** (*expiry date*). An investor who does not wish to take delivery
of the underlying asset (typical for commodities!) must **roll over** (*roll over*) their position: close
the contract near its expiration and open a new one on the next contract. This operation has a cost.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Futures vs Forward"}
The futures is to the forward what a standardized apartment in a condominium is to a custom-built house:
more liquidity and security (thanks to the clearing house), but less flexibility.
:::

### Option (Option)

An **option** (*option*) is a **right** (and not an obligation) to buy (*call option*) or to sell
(*put option*) an asset at a predefined price (*strike price*), at or before a given date (*expiry date*).

Characteristics:

- The option buyer pays a **premium** (*premium*) to acquire this right
- The seller (*writer*) collects the premium and takes the obligation to deliver/buy if the option is exercised
- The option can be **exercised or not** depending on the evolution of the underlying asset price

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — Uses of Options"}
Options are used to:

- **Hedge** (*hedge*) against adverse price movements
- **Speculate** with leverage (*leverage*)
- **Generate income** by selling options (*premium collection strategies*)
:::

### Index (Index)

An **index** (*index*) groups a set of assets into a representative **basket** (*basket*) of a market
or a market segment.

Examples:

- **S&P 500** : the 500 largest US market capitalizations
- **Currency basket** : basket of weighted currencies
- **CAC 40**, **DAX 40**, **SMI** : European equity indices

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
An index makes it possible to measure the overall performance of a market without being exposed to the specific risk of a
single company. ETFs (*Exchange Traded Funds*) make it possible to replicate the performance of an index
at lower cost.
:::

### And Many Other Derivatives...

Financial markets also offer a vast range of **derivatives** (*derivatives*):

- **Swaps** (notably interest rate swaps and FX swaps)
- **CDO** (*Collateralized Debt Obligations*)
- **Warrants**, **certificates**, **turbos**, etc.

These instruments are often used both for **hedging** (*hedging*) and **speculation**.

## Stylised Facts {#sec-stylised-facts}

### Definition

**Stylised facts** (*stylised facts*) are **robust empirical regularities** observed on financial
price and return time series, regardless of the market, frequency or period considered.

Their importance lies in the fact that they **distinguish real markets from a simple random walk** (*random walk*).
A realistic financial model must reproduce these properties.

Main reference: **Cont (2001, 2005)**, *Empirical properties of asset returns*.

### Volatility Clustering (Volatility Clustering)

**Volatility clustering** (*volatility clustering*) is undoubtedly the best known stylised fact.
It was formalized by **Cont (2005)**.

Observation:

- **Large** price variations tend to be followed by **large** variations (in one direction or another)
- **Small** variations tend to be followed by **small** variations

This property implies that **volatility is not constant over time** — we speak of **heteroskedasticity**
(*heteroskedasticity*).

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — The GARCH Model"}
Heteroskedasticity is precisely what the **GARCH** model family (*Generalized Autoregressive
Conditional Heteroskedasticity*) models. The **H** in GARCH directly designates this phenomenon. These models are
ubiquitous in quantitative finance for volatility modeling and forecasting.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
Volatility clustering reflects the fact that markets "get agitated" in episodes: crises and
stress periods are characterized by ample and successive movements, while calm periods
see small movements follow one another. The daily returns of BMW are a clear visual example of this.
:::

### Negative Short-Term Autocorrelation

At **high frequency** (*high frequency*), return series exhibit a **negative autocorrelation**
(*negative autocorrelation*) at short time lags.

This phenomenon was documented by **Cont (2001)** on USD/Yen *tick* data from 1992 to 1994.

Observation:

- At the first lag (*lag 1*), the autocorrelation of price variations is significantly negative
- For subsequent lags, it returns close to zero

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Bid-Ask Bounce"}
This short-term negative autocorrelation is partly explained by the **bid-ask bounce** (*bid-ask bounce*):
transactions alternate between the ask price (*ask*) and the bid price (*bid*), mechanically creating
a positive/negative alternation in price variations.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Contrary to the Medium Term"}
At lower frequencies (daily, weekly), returns are **close to absence of
correlation** — consistent with the weak form of EMH. It is at high frequency that deviations are visible.
:::

### Scaling Laws (Scaling Laws)

**Scaling laws** (*scaling laws*) describe how certain return statistics transform
when changing the time scale.

Formulation:

$$\mathbb{E}[|r|] \sim \Delta t^{\alpha}$$

This relation indicates that the **expected absolute return** evolves as a **power law**
of the time step $\Delta t$, with exponent $\alpha$.

Properties:

- This law is observed over a **wide range of time scales** (from the second to several months)
- It describes how to move from one temporal resolution to another
- It constitutes a form of **self-similarity** (*self-similarity*) of financial markets

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Financial Fractals"}
Scaling laws recall the behavior of **fractals**: by zooming in or out on a financial
price series, one finds similar statistical properties. This contrasts with the simple
random walk where $\alpha = 0.5$ exactly.
:::

### Fat-Tailed Distributions (Fat-Tailed Distributions)

Financial returns do **not follow a normal** (Gaussian) distribution — this is one of the most important stylised facts
for risk management.

The empirical distributions of returns exhibit **fat tails** (*fat tails*, *heavy tails*):

- The **central peak** (*leptokurtosis*) is higher and thinner than that of a Gaussian
- The **tails** of the distribution contain **much more probability** than the Gaussian predicts

::: {.callout-important title="Consequence for Risk Management"}
Extreme events (crashes, flash crashes, crises) are **much more frequent** than the normal law predicts.
A risk model based on normality will systematically underestimate extreme losses.
This is precisely what contributed to the 2008 financial crisis (inadequate risk models).
:::

The empirical distributions resemble **Lévy distributions** (*Lévy distributions*) or
**stable distributions** (*stable distributions*), which have much fatter tails than the
Gaussian.

Illustrative example:

- The probability density of S&P 500 price variations every 30 minutes clearly shows a higher peak
  and fatter tails than the Gaussian distribution of same variance.

### Other Important Stylised Facts

Beyond the four properties presented in detail, markets present other regularities:

**Seasonality** (*seasonality*):

- **Daily**, **weekly**, **monthly** and **annual** seasonal patterns in volumes and volatility
- Market activity is not uniform throughout the day

**Asymmetry in equity markets** (*asymmetry in equity markets*):

- Equity markets tend to fall faster than they rise (*negative skewness*)
- Corrections are often more brutal and faster than rises

**Correlations between spread, volume and volatility**:

- **Negative** correlation between bid-ask spread and volume: the higher the volume, the tighter the spread (*tight spread*)
- **Positive** correlation between volume and volatility: periods of high activity are also periods of high uncertainty

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — Conclusion on Stylised Facts"}
The set of these stylised facts clearly shows that financial markets **do not behave like
simple random walks**. They result from complex human interactions, herding behaviors,
institutional constraints, and non-linear dynamics.
:::

---

## Market Seasonality {#sec-saisonnalite}

### Equity Intraday Seasonality (Equity Daily Seasonality)

Equity markets exhibit a characteristic **intraday seasonality**, documented notably by
**Frijns (2006)** on several exchanges (NYSE, NASDAQ, Paris Bourse).

The intraday profile of volatility or volume presents a characteristic **U-shape** (*U-shape*):

- **Peak at opening** : strong activity and strong volatility from market opening
- **Calm in mid-day** : reduced activity
- **Peak at closing** : renewed activity before market close

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Why the U-Shape?"}
At opening, traders react to news accumulated overnight and adjust their positions.
In mid-day, activity naturally reduces. At closing, traders must close their
daily positions, creating a second activity peak.
:::

This profile is **robust** across different stock markets, although its intensity varies according to
local microstructures (quotation rules, hours, presence of a mid-day fixing).

### FX Intraday Seasonality (FX Daily Seasonality)

The foreign exchange market presents a different intraday seasonality, dictated by **session overlaps**
worldwide (*Masry, 2011*).

The FX market is open 24/7, 5 days a week. Activity follows the successive openings of the major financial centers:

| Session | GMT Hours | Characteristics |
|---------|-----------|-----------------|
| Sydney | 22:00 – 07:00 | Low volume |
| Tokyo | 00:00 – 09:00 | Moderate volume (JPY active) |
| London | 08:00 – 17:00 | **Maximum volume** |
| New York | 13:00 – 22:00 | High volume |

The **major peak** of activity occurs during the **London–New York overlap** (1:00 PM–5:00 PM GMT),
which concentrates the majority of world exchanges.

::: {.callout-note title="Key Takeaway — London-New York Overlap"}
The overlap session between London and New York is the period of **greatest liquidity** and often
of greatest volatility on the foreign exchange market. It is during this window that most
important economic indicators are published.
:::

#### Weekly Seasonality and Influence of Sleep

In-depth research also shows a **weekly seasonality** (*intraweek seasonality*)
on the FX market. Activity peaks repeat at regular intervals during the week,
corresponding to the successive openings of sessions.

The influence of **"sleeping hours"** (sleeping hours by region) on market activity illustrates
that markets are directly driven by the **biological and social cycles of human traders**.

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition"}
FX seasonality is a direct consequence of the fact that the foreign exchange market is global and
decentralized. Activity follows the sun: it moves from Asia to Europe then to America
as the hours pass.
:::

## Market Events {#sec-evenements}

### Classification — Endogenous vs Exogenous

**Market events** (*market events*) are disturbances that generate significant price
movements. They fall into two major categories:

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A["Market Events"] --> B["Endogenous\n(Endogenous)"]
    A --> C["Exogenous\n(Exogenous)"]
    B --> D["Liquidity crunch\n(Liquidity crunch)"]
    C --> E["Scheduled news\n(Scheduled news)"]
    C --> F["Unscheduled news\n(Unscheduled news)"]
```

::: {.callout-note title="Definitions — Endo/Exogenous"}
- **Endogenous** (*endogenous*) : comes from the **inside** of the system — the cause arises from the market itself
- **Exogenous** (*exogenous*) : comes from the **outside** — external information or shock impacts the market
:::

### Endogenous Events

Endogenous events result from the **internal dynamics** of the market, without identifiable external cause.

The main example is the **liquidity crunch** (*liquidity crunch*):

- Numerous sellers find no buyers (or vice versa)
- Prices collapse (or soar) not because of economic news, but because of an imbalance between supply and demand for liquidity
- The **Flash Crash** of 2010 is an example of a partly endogenous event, amplified by trading algorithms

### Exogenous Events — Scheduled News

**Scheduled news** (*scheduled news*) are economic publications whose date and time
are announced in advance. They generate predictable volatility spikes.

Important examples:

- **Non-Farm Payrolls (NFP)** : published every **first Friday of the month at 8:30 AM EST** (2:30 PM Swiss time) — measure of US employment excluding the agricultural sector. This is one of the most anticipated indicators and generates the strongest reaction on the foreign exchange market.
- **GDP** (*Gross Domestic Product*, GDP) : quarterly publication of economic growth data by country
- **Consumption indices** : consumer confidence, home sales, durable goods orders, etc.
- **Interest rate decisions** by central banks (Fed, ECB, SNB...)

::: {.callout-important title="Trading the News — A Major Challenge"}
Scheduled news are known in advance, but their **content** is uncertain. Markets
already anticipate an expected value (*consensus*). What matters is not the absolute published figure,
but the **deviation from expectations** (*surprise*). A good figure below expectations can make a market fall.
:::

### Exogenous Events — Unscheduled News

**Unscheduled news** (*unscheduled news*) are, by definition, unpredictable. Their impact
is generally more violent because markets cannot prepare for them.

Historical examples:

- **September 2011** : the Swiss National Bank (SNB) unilaterally sets a **floor** (*floor*) of 1.20 CHF for EUR/CHF, generating an immediate rise of several percent of the Swiss franc in a few seconds
- **September 11, 2001 terrorist attack** in Manhattan: closure of US exchanges, global market collapse at reopening
- Natural disasters, nuclear accidents, surprise political decisions...

::: {.callout-warning title="Risk Management in the Face of Unscheduled Events"}
Unscheduled events illustrate the **limit of risk models**: no model can anticipate
a terrorist attack or a surprise central bank decision. Risk management must provide protection mechanisms
against the unknown (*tail risk hedging*, *black swan events*).
:::

### Quantification of Market Events

Academic research, notably that of **T. Bisig (2012)**, has sought to **quantify and classify**
market events on high-frequency EUR/USD data.

The methodology consists in:

- Measuring the **magnitude** (*magnitude*) of each event — that is, the extent of the price movement
- Analyzing the **temporal profile** of the reaction — immediate or gradual
- Superimposing magnitude and price around the time of the event

The graphs illustrate real events occurring on the EUR/USD pair between 2007 and 2009, showing
that each major event leaves a **characteristic footprint** on high-frequency data.

::: {.callout-tip title="Intuition — Utility of Quantification"}
Being able to automatically identify and quantify market events in high-frequency data makes it possible to clean data (for statistical models), estimate the impact of news,
and potentially build *event-driven* trading strategies.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways {#sec-cles}

::: {.callout-note title="Market Efficiency (EMH)"}
- Fama's theory (1960, Nobel 2013): prices reflect all available information
- Three forms: **weak** (past prices), **semi-strong** (public information), **strong** (all information)
- Widely criticized: speculative bubbles, Flash Crash, herding behaviors testify to real inefficiencies
- **No consensus** : EMH remains a useful framework, not an absolute truth
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Trading Venues and Instruments"}
- **Regulated markets** (*exchanges*) : centralized, strict surveillance, clearing house → less risky
- **OTC** (*Over The Counter*) : decentralized, market makers, less transparent → riskier
- Instruments: **spot**, **forward**, **futures** (standardized), **options** (right, not obligation), **indices**
- The **roll over** of futures is crucial to avoid physical delivery
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Volumes"}
- **NYSE Euronext US** : largest world exchange by volume (~6 900 Bn USD in 2013)
- **Forex** : the largest market on the planet (~5 000 Bn USD/day)
- **EUR/USD** : 25 % of world FX volume · ~3.6 M USD exchanged per second
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Stylised Facts — Markets Are Not Random Walks"}
- **Volatility clustering** : large variations follow large variations (→ GARCH)
- **Negative autocorrelation** at short term / high frequency
- **Scaling laws** : $\mathbb{E}[|r|] \sim \Delta t^{\alpha}$
- **Fat tails** (*fat tails*) : extreme events are much more frequent than the normal law predicts
- **Seasonality** : daily (U-shape for equities; sessions for FX), weekly, monthly
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Market Events"}
- **Endogenous** : born from the market itself (liquidity crunch)
- **Scheduled exogenous** : NFP, GDP, interest rate decisions → anticipated volatility
- **Unscheduled exogenous** : terrorist attacks, surprise central bank decisions → brutal and unpredictable impact
- The quantification of events (Bisig, 2012) enables their systematic analysis on high-frequency data
:::
